title: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI: the Flood
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.4, Poem of Gilgamesh (ed. A. R. George, rev. G. Rozzi and E. Jiménez), SB XI) + English of the eBL edition (A. R. George (eBL edition))
description: Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI: 329 of 329 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (5 British Museum tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and A. R. George's English translation.
introduction:
Uta-napishti tells how the god Ea warned him of the Flood, how he built a boat, survived the deluge, sent out birds, and was granted eternal life. Gilgamesh fails a test of sleep, obtains a plant of rejuvenation, loses it to a snake, and returns to Uruk.

The Standard Babylonian version of the epic, traditionally ascribed to the scholar Sin-leqi-unninni, was written on twelve tablets. Most surviving copies come from the libraries of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th century BCE) and from Babylon and other Babylonian cities (7th-2nd century BCE). This page gives Tablet XI in the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition by A. R. George (2022 and later revisions).

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/4/SB/XI) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed manuscript with the most signs preserved there. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives. Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 329 of the 329 lines of the eBL edition (100%), from 5 tablets in the British Museum: K.2252 (Nineveh), K.8517 (Nineveh), Sm.2131 (Nineveh), K.7752 (Nineveh), K.3375 (Nineveh).
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition (based on A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford 2003). Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

translation.text:
5I was fully intent on doing battle with you,
6[but] in your presence my hand is stayed.
7How was it you attended the gods’ assembly, and found life?’
8Ūta-napišti spoke to him, to Gilgameš:
9‘I will disclose to you, Gilgameš, a secret matter,
10and I will tell you a mistery of the gods.
11The city of Šuruppak – a city you yourself know,
12the [city that] is situated on the [banks] of the Euphrates–
13that city was old and the gods were within it,
14(when) the great gods decided to cause the Deluge.
15Their father Anu took the oath,
16their counsellor, the hero Enlil;
17their chamberlain, Ninurta,
18their inspector of waterways, Ennugi
19With them the Prince Ea was under oath likewise,
20(but) repeated their words to a reed fence:
21“Reed fence, reed fence! Brick wall, brick wall!
22Listen, O reed fence! Pay heed, O brick wall!
23O man of Šuruppak, son of Ubār-Tutu,
24demolish the house, build a boat!
25Abandon riches and seek survival!
26Spurn property and save life!
27Put on board the boat the seed of all living creatures!
28The boat that you are going to build,
29her dimensions should all be matching:
30her breadth and length should be the same,
31cover her with a roof, like the Apsû”.
32I understood and spoke to Ea my master:
33“I hereby concur, my lord, with what you told me thus.

36Ea opened his mouth to speak,
37saying to me, his servant:

279‘You came here, Gilgameš, toiled, exerted yourself,
280what have I given you as you go back to your land?
281I will disclose, Gilgameš, a secret matter,
282and [I will] tell you a mystery of [the gods.]
283It is a plant, its [appearance] is like box-thorn,
284its thorn is like the dog-rose’s, it will [prick your hands.]
285If you can gain possession of that plant,
286[you’ll be again as you were in your youth.]’
287When Gilgameš heard this,
288he opened a [channel] …
289Heavy stones he tied [on his feet,]
290they dragged him down to the Apsû […]
291He pulled the plant, and pulled [it up and lifted it,]
292he cut loose the heavy stones [from his feet.]
293The sea cast him up on its shore.
294Gilgameš spoke to him, to Ur-šanābi the boatman:
295‘Ur-šanābi, this plant is the “plant of the heart-beat”,
296by which means a man can recapture his vitality.
297I will take it to Uruk the sheepfold,
298I will feed some to an old man and put the plant to the test.
299If the old man grows young (again),
300I will eat some myself and go back to how I was in my youth!'
301At twenty leagues they broke bread,
